newsitem.title: CHINA: Kuehne & Nagel to double Asian business in three years.
newsitem.headline: Kuehne & Nagel to double Asian business in three years.

text.p: Kuehne & Nagel International AG aims to double sales volume across its Asia Pacific network within three years, regional sales and marketing director, Claus Czisla, has told Reuters.
One productivity initiative underway is intensive training by Swedish consultantcy firm Mercuri of 200 of the company's sales team to improve sea and air freight selling techniques.

"We are trying to improve efficiency and productivity. I think we have been quite succesful up to now but we think because of the concentration process in the freight forwarding industry we have to grow very fast to be one of the bigger firms," Czisla said.

Last year, Kuehne & Nagel's Asia Pacific division handled 137,424 TEU of seafreight imports and 48,187 of seafreight exports along with 57,897 tonnes of airfreight exports and 51,978 tonnes of airfreight imports.
Czisla said year on year growth has been impressive.

Airfreight exports handled totalled 24,951 tonnes in 1993, 30,169 in 1994 and 37,311 in 1995. In airfreight imports, regional business has grown from 22,180 tonnes in 1993 to 32,352 in 1994 and 40,353 in 1995, the statistics showed.
"Last year was a very good year volume wise but margins are really under threat. Seafreight rates especially are cut-throat and have been halved in three years," he added.
Czisla's Asia Pacific sales area extends from Japan to Pakistan and Chnna to New Zealand employing 1,700 people in 50 offices. Expansion is planned, especially in India.
"We have eight offices in India at the moment. Within the next one or two years we think we will open up another seven or eight offices," Czisla said.

Kuehne & Nagel also wants to concentrate on setting up logistics platforms in China, the first is expected to be in Shanghai, to provide value added services such as quality control and specialised packing.
Rising costs in Asia, 10 to 15 per cent a year in Hong Kong, for instance, continued to be a major worry.
"On the one hand you have deteriorating profit margins, on the other you have rising costs," Czisla said.
Czisla forecast more mergers among smaller freight forwarders because the emphasis is now on having access to a global network.

"I think we will definitely see big, well established companies merging, Firms of around 5-6,000 employees are simply too small so sooner or later they will merge or enter alliances because they need a global network and you need so much volume to be successful," Czisla said. - Reuters Air Cargo Service Tel+ 44 171 542 7706 Fax +5017 - www.racs.com
